content: In 2017, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), Operational Centre Amsterdam, received 8 million euros from the Dutch Postcode Lottery, and this funding remains active. Dr. Michael Rich is employed by Partners in Health, where he contributes to the development of clinical care guidelines and programmatic management of drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB). He also serves as a consultant for the World Health Organization (WHO) on DR-TB treatment for national TB programs. Additionally, he conducts research and develops treatment regimens for DR-TB as part of the UNITAID-funded Expand New Drug Markets for TB (EndTB) project, which was active during the formulation of the current recommendations. Dr. Rada Savic participated as a panel member in the WHO Meeting on Target Regimen Profiles, receiving a fee of $2,500. She also reviewed grants for the European and Developing Countries Clinical Trials Partnership, valued at $1,000. Furthermore, she is a principal or co-principal investigator on research grants funded by the United States National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the Gates Foundation, focusing on improving TB treatment options. All these activities are currently active. The External Review Group (ERG) members, including Essam Elmoghazi, James Johnston, Enos Masini, Rohit Sarin, Kitty van Weezenbeek, Irina Vasilyeva, and Piret Viiklepp, declared no conflicts of interest related to the objectives of the meeting. Some ERG members were involved in unrelated clinical trials, and no restrictions were applied to their participation as expert reviewers. Dr. Charles L. Daley serves as the chair and member of data monitoring committees for delamanid studies, receiving $45,000 over eight years from Otsuka Pharmaceutical (ongoing). He also chaired a data monitoring committee for clofazimine studies, receiving $2,500 from Novartis (completed in 2016). Ingrid Oxley, a healthcare worker who has experienced two episodes of TB, advocated for the treatment of latent TB infection (LTBI) among healthcare workers during the 2015 Union Conference in Cape Town. Many members of TB Proof, an organization of healthcare workers, may have benefited from WHO guidelines for LTBI treatment or received funding for LTBI treatment, though this was not the focus of the current guideline. Dr. Simon Schaaf received research support for pharmacokinetics studies on second-line TB medicines in children, funded by the NIH and Otsuka Pharmaceutical (approximately ZAR 5 million/year). The NIH grant ended in 2015, but the Otsuka grant remains active. Dr. Helen Stagg received a grant from Otsuka Pharmaceutical (£59,925; 2013–2015) for consultancy work on MDR-TB clinical pathways in Eastern Europe. She also received funding for the HALT study on hepatitis and LTBI from the UK Department of Health and the National Institute for Health Research (£86,000 in 2014; £315,265 for fellowship, salary, and research costs; 2015–2017). Sanofi provided free rifapentine for the HALT study participants (2014–2017). Additionally, she received an International Trainee Scholarship Award ($1,000) at the 2016 American Thoracic Society conference, where she presented a review she conducted. Dr. Carlos A. Torres-Duque, a member of the National Advisory Committee for Tuberculosis in Colombia, contributes to updates of national TB treatment guidelines. His expert opinion is based on evidence and experience and does not generate personal profits. Independent evidence reviewers, including Narges Alipanah, Cecily Miller, Payam Nahid (team leader for PICO 1, 2, and 7–10), Leila Chaisson, Richard Menzies (team leader for PICO 3, 4, and 6), James Johnston, Gregory Fox (team leader for PICO 11), and Jennifer Ho, conducted systematic reviews of evidence for this revision. They declared no conflicts of interest related to the policy guideline objectives. Dr. Payam Nahid declared that his research unit received support from the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) through a federal contract to support clinical trial units in San Francisco, USA, and Hanoi, Vietnam. The WHO guidelines for the treatment of drug-susceptible tuberculosis and patient care (2017 update) were developed in accordance with WHO's conflict of interest policy. All contributors completed a WHO Declaration of Interest form, which was reviewed by the steering group to identify potential financial or intellectual conflicts of interest. In some cases, conflicts justified exclusion from the Guideline Development Group (GDG), and decisions were made in consultation with the WHO Global TB Programme Director, the WHO Guideline Review Committee, and the WHO Legal Office. The GDG included representatives from technical partners, academia, national TB program managers, civil society organizations, WHO collaborating centers, professional organizations, and the International Organization for Migration. Biographies of GDG members were made public before the meeting, and the WHO Guidelines Steering Committee reviewed the declarations of interest at the start of the meeting. Several GDG members declared no conflicts of interest, while others declared interests that were judged not to conflict with the meeting's objectives. For example, Dr. Daniela Cirillo received funding from FIND and Otsuka for drug-susceptibility testing evaluations and leads a supranational TB reference laboratory in Italy. Dr. Charles L. Daley received funding from Otsuka for chairing data monitoring committees for delamanid trials. Dr. Kelly Dooley received funding for expert advice on trial design and participated in various TB-related clinical trials. Dr. Agnes Gebhard works for the KNCV TB Foundation, which has projects funded by the Eli Lilly Foundation and collaborates with Cepheid on GeneXpert machine installations and training. Dr. Carlos Torres-Duque received honoraria from Janssen Pharmaceuticals for presentations on TB prevention and WHO policy on bedaquiline. Dr. Tom Shinnick, an employee of the CDC, declared that his travel and research related to TB laboratory services are supported by the CDC. He served on the Data and Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) for a delamanid clinical trial organized by Otsuka without receiving remuneration. Some GDG members, such as Lindsay McKenna and José A. Caminero, were recused from specific discussions due to potential conflicts of interest. For example, McKenna's organization received non-commercial support from various entities, and Caminero is a consultant for the International Union Against Tuberculosis and Lung Disease, which is involved in implementing shorter MDR-TB regimens. The ERG members, including Chen-Yuan Chiang, Celine Garfin, Michael Kimerling, Vaira Leimane, Gao Mengqiu, Norbert Ndjeka, Ejaz Qadeer, Lee Reichman, Rohit Sarin, and Irina Vasilyeva, declared no conflicts of interest related to the meeting's objectives. Two ERG members, Guy Marks and another unnamed individual, declared interests that were judged not to conflict with the guidelines' objectives. Marks received research support from AERAS for evaluating latent TB infection and TB recurrence rates in Vietnam.
